note: Original post did not expose a complete repeatable prompt. Treat this as a real showcase post, not a verified tutorial.
originalText:
The US government just banned one of the most powerful AI models ever built.

3 days after launch.

Here's the full story. 👇

——

Anthropic launched Fable 5 and Mythos 5 — its most advanced AI models to date — on June 9th.

They underwent thousands of hours of testing with government agencies and third-party researchers before release.

72 hours later, the US Commerce Department pulled the plug.

——

The timeline:

→ Jun 9: Fable 5 and Mythos 5 launch publicly; described as state-of-the-art across industry benchmarks

→ Jun 12: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick issues an export control directive at 5:21 PM ET

→ Same day: Anthropic disables both models for ALL users worldwide to ensure compliance

——

What the order actually says:

→ No foreign national can access Fable 5 or Mythos 5
→ This includes foreign nationals inside the US
→ This includes Anthropic's own foreign-national employees
→ The letter gave zero specific details on the security concern
→ All other Anthropic models (Claude Opus, Sonnet etc.) are unaffected

——

Why? The government claims someone discovered a way to jailbreak Fable 5.

Fable 5 is built on Mythos; a model so powerful it was previously only available to a small group of trusted organizations under a classified cybersecurity program called Project Glasswing.

The jailbreak would theoretically unlock Mythos's full cybersecurity capabilities through Fable 5's public interface.

——

Anthropic's response:

"We reviewed a demonstration of this specific technique; it unlocks capabilities in only one specific instance, not a universal bypass of all safeguards. The cybersecurity capabilities cited are already available in competing frontier AI systems."

Translation: they think the government is overreacting.

——

The bigger picture nobody's talking about:

→ This is the first time the US has used export controls to ban a domestic AI model
→ Anthropic is weeks away from a reported $965B IPO filing
→ Fable 5 customers lost access with zero warning
→ The ban includes Anthropic's own non-citizen engineers; they can't use their own product

——

Anthropic says it's a "misunderstanding" and is working to restore access.

The Commerce Department has not responded.

As of right now; Fable 5 is dark.

#Fable5 #Anthropic #AINews #NationalSecurity #Mythos5 #AIRegulation

title: Autonomous agent workflow for Fable 5
author: Sitam Meur
verification: Fetched from X via twitter-cli from global-search; original author and post URL preserved.
note: Original post did not expose a complete repeatable prompt. Treat this as a real showcase post, not a verified tutorial.
originalText:
"I don't prompt Claude anymore. I have loops running that prompt Claude. My job is to write loops." — @bcherny, head of Claude Code at @AnthropicAI 

A loop finds the work, hands it to an agent, checks the result, logs what's done, and decides what's next without you in the middle. You're not prompting anymore. The system is.

Engineers have been building versions of this for years. What's new is that it ships inside the tools now. And the model inside the loop finally got good enough to make it actually work.

That second part is the missing piece. A well-designed loop with a weak model still fails; it makes safe bets instead of structural ones, stores failure notes instead of verified learnings, and rarely consults what it figured out in the last session.

@RLanceMartin tested Claude Fable 5 inside exactly these loops:

→ 6x more pipeline improvements than Opus 4.7 
→ Memory verification coverage jumped from 17% to 73% 
→ Persistent memory improved Fable 5's performance 3x more than Opus 4.8

Stripe compressed months of engineering into a single day, a codebase-wide migration across 50M lines of Ruby that would've taken a whole team over two months by hand.

Anthropic's finding: the longer and more complex the task, the larger Fable 5's lead over every other model.

That's not a coincidence. That's what a model built for loops looks like.

At the highest effort, Fable 5 reflects on and validates its own work, and that's exactly what makes highly autonomous operations possible.

Loop engineering is trending. But it was always the destination. We just didn't have the model that could survive the loop long enough to matter.

Now we do. 👇

title: Fable 5 benchmark results compared with other models
author: Shruti Tiwari
verification: Fetched from X via twitter-cli from global-search; original author and post URL preserved.
note: Original post did not expose a complete repeatable prompt. Treat this as a real showcase post, not a verified tutorial.
originalText:
Everyone is talking about Fable 5's benchmarks.

I think Anthropic accidentally revealed something much bigger.

For the first time, a frontier AI company publicly shipped:

the same model with different levels of access.

Fable 5 and Mythos 5 share the same underlying intelligence.

Same brain.

Different permissions.

Read that again.

The biggest shift isn't that models are getting smarter.

It's that access is becoming a product.

For years the AI race looked like this:

Build smarter model → Give everyone smarter model.

Now it looks like this:

Build smarter model → Decide who gets the unrestricted version.

That's a completely different future.

Look closely at this infographic.

The most important benchmark isn't SWE-Bench.

It's not FrontierCode.

It's not the coding scores.

It's the fact that Anthropic built an entirely separate program around Mythos.

Trusted access.

Glasswing partners.

Cybersecurity organizations.

Biology researchers.

Permission layers.

Why?

Because these models are starting to operate less like chatbots...

and more like autonomous workers.

A model that can compress months of engineering into days.

A model that can conduct week-long research projects.

A model that can coordinate complex workflows across massive codebases.

That's what Mythos represents.

And Fable is essentially the public version of that future.

The strange part?

We're no longer asking:

"Which model is smartest?"

We're starting to ask:

"Who gets access to the smartest model?"

That might end up being the biggest AI story of 2026.

title: Prompt-driven motion or animation demo
author: MarkWeekly
verification: Fetched from X via twitter-cli from global-search; original author and post URL preserved.
note: Original post did not expose a complete repeatable prompt. Treat this as a real showcase post, not a verified tutorial.
originalText:
Two unrelated things happened this week that turned out to be the same thing at different layers.

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5 on June 9. Fifth-generation model. Positioned directly at "the hardest knowledge work and coding problems." $10/M input, $50/M output, 90% prompt cache discount. The Every team ran a week of testing. The signal in the positioning isn't subtle: the model itself is now the native executor of the task. Not a component in a pipeline. The whole pipeline.

Then I watched Ruben Casas from Postman speak at AI Engineer on generative UI for MCP apps. His core question: frontier models already write better frontend code than most engineers do by hand, so why is almost every agent UI still calling prebuilt React component libraries?

He laid out three tiers.

Static — call predefined components. Fast, rigid. AG UI and Goose's auto visualizer live here.
Declarative — LLM generates JSON or YAML, a runtime engine maps to components. He called this the most pragmatic balance point today.
Generative — LLM writes HTML, CSS, JavaScript directly. No component layer at all. His weather agent demo: one tool call, a search box, blur animations, accessibility on by default. No React. No template. Generated from context.

The critical constraint for generative UI is containment. LLM-generated code must run inside a sandbox. That's exactly why MCP apps default to a double iframe architecture. It's not over-engineering. It's the prerequisite for shipping generative UI to production.

His closing analogy: the first TV programs were just radio shows with a camera pointed at them, because nobody could yet imagine what television should look like. Agent UI in June 2026 is that moment.

Three layers are moving in the same direction simultaneously.

Model layer: Fable 5 takes the whole task directly. No manual decomposition into small chunks to feed the model piece by piece.

UI layer: Generative UI stops asking which React component the model should call. The system's job becomes sandbox + constraints, not maintaining a component library.

Workflow layer where I live every day: I built the early https://t.co/2oU9IRNgBi Playground with a React component library for rendering finding cards. Each finding got a card, severity got a color badge, category got an icon. Looked clean. But credential exposure and prompt injection both graded High Severity, and they read identically — the component spec flattened the nuance. The standardization was actually erasing information.

Switched to letting LLM render the cards directly with a sandbox constraint: SKILL.md can't execute shell, can't access /etc, output must be markdown. Everything else belongs to the model. After that change, https://t.co/2oU9IRNgBi finally looked like an AI-native product instead of a SaaS with an AI wrapper.

Components are dissolving into two things: generation and sandbox. Model handles generation. System sets the boundary. That's what composability actually means in the AI era. Not assembling parts. Building the right cage for the model to play in.

If you're building something right now, map each layer. Which parts are still assembling components, which parts are already generation + sandbox. The component-assembly layers aren't assets. The sandbox design is.
